catalog_locator: Bôt 2011a: p. 89, §0 Introduction, first paragraph. Bouh 2004: thesis p. 38, §III and §III.1.
catalog_quote: [Bôt 2011a, p. 89] Le yasa est une langue bantu de la côte équatoriale parlée au Cameroun et en Guinée équatoriale par dix milliers de locuteurs. Il s'agit d'une langue à classes, d'une langue à tons: deux tons ponctuels (haut et bas) et deux tons modulés (descendant et montant) dont la structure syllabique de base est de type (consonne) + voyelle (C) V. [Bouh 2004, p. 38] En yasa, les unités suprasegmentales sont les tons. On appelle ton, la hauteur musicale de la voix pendant la production d'un son. ... Le ton distinctif est la hauteur musicale de la voix qui permet de faire la différence dans le sens des mots. La langue yasa dénombre, quatre tonèmes: le tonème haut, le tonème bas, le tonème ascendant et le tonème descendant.

new_statements.quote: Le yasa est une langue bantu de la côte équatoriale parlée au Cameroun et en Guinée équatoriale par dix milliers de locuteurs. Il s'agit d'une langue à classes, d'une langue à tons : deux tons ponctuels (haut et bas) et deux tons modulés (descendant et montant) dont la structure syllabique de base est de type (consonne) + voyelle (C) V.
new_statements.translation: Yasa is a Bantu language of the equatorial coast spoken in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea by some ten thousand speakers. It is a noun-class language and a tone language: two level tones (high and low) and two contour tones (falling and rising), whose basic syllable structure is of the type (consonant) + vowel, (C)V.
new_statements.citation: Bôt, Dieudonné Martin Luther. 2011a. Les verbes dérivés du yasa. Journal of West African Languages 38(1): 89–98 (Université de Douala).
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (10 pp., text, JWAL XXXVIII.1 2011; p. 1 = journal p. 89, p. 2 carries running head '90 Journal of West African Languages XXXVIII.1 (2011)'). §0 INTRODUCTION, first paragraph, reads verbatim: "Le yasa est une langue bantu de la côte équatoriale parlée au Cameroun et en Guinée équatoriale par dix milliers de locuteurs. Il s'agit d'une langue à classes, d'une langue à tons : deux tons ponctuels (haut et bas) et deux tons modulés (descendant et montant) dont la structure syllabique de base est de type (consonne) + voyelle (C) V." Exact match with the reported quote. Surrounding section (pp. 89–91) gives verb-radical tone schemes H-B, B-B, B-H, and rules R1 (vow…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yasa is described as a tone language with two level tonemes (H, L) and two contour tonemes (falling, rising); every syllable carries a tone and grammatical alternations are tonal (floating-tone docking, tone reduction, tone assimilation). Neither this article nor its companion (Bôt 2011b, p. 99: 'Langue à tons au sens de Welmers (1975:90)') says anything about word stress or accent; no source examined states a stress position or explicitly denies stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: verb radicals show mainly H-L, L-L and L-H patterns (p. 89–90); floating L of an elided prefix docks on the following vowel producing rising or double-low tone (2011a p. 90–91; 2011b §4.11–4.12).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the language's prosodic type, illustrated with citation forms (infinitives with prefix e-, nouns with class prefix) and short phrases; word- vs phrase-level prominence is not addressed. Source is a generative morphophonology article, not a full phonology; the author's 1992 thesis 'Phonologie générative du yasa' is the primary phonology and was not obtainable.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Yasa/Iyasa of the Campo–Kribi coast of Cameroon (Bôt: Campo arrondissement and across the Ntem in Equatorial Guinea; Bouh 2004: informants incl. Oscar Makou; Belew: Campo/Ebodje), i.e. yasa1242 itself, not a differently named variety. Glottolog's descriptive list for yasa1242 includes a misattached entry (Polomé 1997, 'Notes on the dwarfs in Germanic tradition'), which is irrelevant. Kombe/Ndowe (Equatorial Guinea) is a closely related but separate languoid and was not used.

sources.note: p. 89: Yasa is 'une langue à tons : deux tons ponctuels (haut et bas) et deux tons modulés (descendant et montant)'; verb radical tone patterns H-B, B-B, B-H most attested (pp. 89–90); tone rules (atterrissage, réduction, assimilation). No mention of stress/accent anywhere.

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Only the first 34 scanned pages (thesis pp. i–33) could be recovered, from a Common Crawl capture (CC-MAIN-2023-50) truncated at 1 MiB of 2.7 MB; rebuilt PDF + scanned text. Chapter I 'Aperçu phonologique' (from p. 17) covers vowels and consonants; the tone section lies past the truncation. The abbreviation/symbol list (pp. 13–14) marks ton haut, ton bas, ton montant, ton descendant and sequences B-B, H-H. No 'accent' in the recovered pages. The original rogerblench.info host is dead (not reachable by automated download / domain repurposed); web.archive.org holds a full copy (20240724052320)…

sources.citation: Belew, Anna K. 2020. Sociolinguistic documentation of language shift and maintenance in Iyasa. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Mānoa. iv+185 pp.
sources.note: Sociolinguistic; nothing on stress. Only notes that the CELI orthography uses 'diacritics to mark tone in Iyasa' and that tone minimal pairs exist (p. 147). §2.2 (p. 3) and p. 110 list the existing descriptions: Bouh Ma Sitna 2004, Lonfo 2009 (MA thesis with a phonology sketch), Bôt 2011a/b, an unpublished 200-page grammar by Cyrille Bothe, and Braden Brown's Buffalo dissertation research.
